title: Blogging is the New Resume: why writing beats a resume for non-technical roles
summary: Ryan Hoover argues that resumes poorly communicate ability, and that blogging does what GitHub does for developers: it shows how you think. He shares how a year of writing built a network that produced job offers and seeded the Product Hunt launch, then lists the caveats of blogging.

principles.text: Show your thinking publicly instead of telling it on a resume; blogging reveals thought process and culture fit.
principles.quote: Blogging is an effective way to illustrate expertise, personality, and most importantly, thought process.

principles.text: Writing builds a network that creates opportunities when you need them, including jobs and founder intros.
principles.quote: When I announced my departure without a plan, the network I grew from blogging, reached out with support.

principles.text: Seed a new product's community with relationships earned through your writing.
principles.quote: We seeded the community largely with relationships formed through my writing, inviting several dozen well-respected startup founders, investors, and product people to participate.

principles.text: Blogging only works if you enjoy it; intrinsic motivation is what sustains it.
principles.quote: If you’re not intrinsically motivated to do so, you’ll quit.

principles.text: Treat blogging as a long-term investment: accept that early posts won't go viral and that quantity leads to quality.
principles.quote: First, you must accept that most people don’t care what you think and that quantity leads to quality.

principles.text: Write about genuine passions, not trending topics, and don't make every post self-promotion.
principles.quote: You should write about growth hacking if you’re genuinely passionate about it.
